title: There is a reason the enemy did not begin with Adam.
paragraphs: There is a reason the enemy did not begin with Adam.
That detail has haunted theologians, historians, rabbis, and believers for centuries.

Out of all the creatures in Eden…
Out of all the moments in human history…
Out of all the strategies hell could have used…
the serpent went to Eve first.
Not because she was weaker.
But because the enemy understood something most people still do not.
The first attack in human history was not against strength.

It was against identity.
Against trust.
Against sacred intimacy with God.
And if you are not careful, you will read Genesis too quickly and completely miss the psychological warfare unfolding beneath the surface.
Because the story in Eden was never simply about fruit.
It was about worship.
It was about authority.
It was about whose voice humanity would trust.
And some of you are still fighting that same serpent every single day.
The book of Genesis introduces the serpent with chilling precision:
“Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made.” — Genesis 3:1
The Hebrew word for “subtil” is עָרוּם (ʿārûm).

It means:
crafty,
shrewd,
strategic,
psychologically calculating.
This was not a wild beast attacking randomly.
This was an intelligent spiritual assassination.

The serpent studies.
The serpent watches.
The serpent waits.
Hell does not waste temptation.

It studies wounds.
Patterns.
Loneliness.
Silence.
Insecurities.
Fatigue.
Curiosity.
Isolation.
And then it whispers.
The Hebrew text becomes even more revealing when the serpent approaches Eve:
“Yea, hath God said…” — Genesis 3:1

In Hebrew:
אַף כִּי־אָמַר אֱלֹהִים
(ʾaph kî-ʾāmar ʾĕlōhîm)
The structure carries the tone of manipulation and distortion.
It was not a direct denial at first.
It was suggestion.
Subtle reframing.
The enemy rarely begins with rebellion.
He begins with confusion.
He introduces uncertainty into what God already made clear.
That is still how darkness operates today.
Not usually through obvious evil.
But through altered truth.

“Did God really say purity matters?”
“Did God really say forgiveness is necessary?”
“Did God really say marriage is sacred?”
“Did God really say obedience matters?”
“Did God really say you are loved?”
The first satanic strategy in history was theological distortion.
And Eve was standing in the middle of it.
But here is where the story becomes deeply emotional.
Most people assume Eve was targeted because she was gullible.
Scripture never says that.
Not once.
In fact, the text suggests something far more devastating.
Eve was targeted because she carried influence.
When Satan attacked humanity, he did not go first to the one formed from dust.
He went to the one created from intimacy.
Genesis 2:22 says:
“And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman…”
The Hebrew word for “rib” is צֵלָע (ṣēlāʿ).
It does not simply mean rib bone.
It can also mean side, chamber, support structure, sacred architecture.

Eve was not created beneath Adam.
Not from his feet to be trampled.
Not from his head to dominate him.
From his side.
Near his heart.

Close enough to protect.
Close enough to love.
Close enough to reflect divine companionship.
The first woman carried relational power.
She represented connection.
And Satan understood something terrifying:

If he could fracture trust inside the relationship…
he could fracture humanity itself.
So the serpent did not begin with brute force.
He began with conversation.
Notice something else most people overlook.
The serpent speaks to Eve while she is separated from Adam.
Isolation has always been one of hell’s favorite environments.
Because voices become louder when accountability disappears.
That is why so many spiritual collapses happen in secret.

Private compromises.
Hidden addictions.
Silent bitterness.
Unspoken wounds.
The enemy loves isolated minds.
1 Peter 5:8 says:
“Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.”
The Greek word for “devour” is καταπιεῖν (katapiein).

It means:
to swallow whole,
to consume completely.
Satan never wanted Eve slightly distracted.
He wanted humanity consumed.
And then comes the most dangerous sentence in Eden.
“You shall not surely die.” — Genesis 3:4

In Hebrew:
לֹא־מוֹת תְּמֻתוּן
(lō-mōṯ təmuṯūn)
This was the first direct contradiction of God in human history.

The serpent moves from questioning God…
to replacing God.
And humanity has been wrestling with that temptation ever since.

To redefine morality.
To edit truth.
To crown personal desire above divine authority.
This is why the fall was catastrophic.
Because sin was not merely eating forbidden fruit.
Sin was humanity choosing autonomy over intimacy with God.
And suddenly shame enters the world.
Genesis 3:7 says:
“And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked…”
The Hebrew word for naked here is עֵירֹם (ʿêrōm).
Not merely physically exposed.

Vulnerable.
Ashamed.
Stripped.
Emotionally uncovered.
Sin always promises elevation.
But delivers exposure.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.

The hidden habit.
The fake smile.
The secret compromise.
The late-night regret.
The exhausting performance.
The fear that if people truly knew you, they would walk away.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because while Adam and Eve hid…
God came looking.
Genesis 3:9:
“And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?”

In Hebrew:
אַיֶּכָּה
(ʾayyekkāh)
Not because God lacked information.
But because God was inviting confession.
That question still echoes through every generation.

Where are you spiritually?
Where are you emotionally?
Where are you in your obedience?
Where are you in your secret life?
Where are you in your relationship with Christ?
Some of you reading this have mastered pretending.
But heaven still sees the hiding places.
And yet…
God still comes searching.
That is the part that breaks me every time.
Humanity sinned.
Humanity hid.
Humanity blamed.
Humanity fractured.
But God pursued.
Even in judgment, mercy appeared.
Genesis 3:15 contains what theologians call the Protoevangelium — the first Gospel prophecy.
Speaking to the serpent, God says:
“And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.”
The Hebrew word for “bruise/crush” is שׁוּף (šūp̄).

Crush.
Strike fatally.
This was the first prophetic announcement of Jesus Christ.

Before humanity ever escaped Eden…
God already revealed redemption.
The serpent would wound the Messiah temporarily…
but Christ would crush the serpent ultimately.
That is why the cross terrified hell.
Because Satan thought Eden was victory.
But Calvary became reversal.
Jesus became the second Adam.

Where Adam failed in a garden…
Christ surrendered in a garden.

Where humanity hid in shame…
Jesus was publicly stripped on a cross.

Where the serpent brought death through a tree…
Christ brought life through a tree.
And maybe that is why this story still wrecks people emotionally.
Because deep down, we recognize ourselves in Eve.
We know what it feels like to hear conflicting voices.

We know temptation.
Curiosity.
Confusion.
Shame.
Fear.
Hiding.
But we also recognize the voice of God still calling into our darkness:
“Where are you?”
Not to destroy us.
To bring us home.
Be honest.
This hit harder than some of you expected.
And somebody you know desperately needs this reminder that the enemy’s oldest weapon is still deception… but Christ is still greater.

The serpent spoke first in Eden…
but God gets the final word.
